sentences.text: Estimates place the length of this dinosaur at 2.85 meters and its mass at 63 kilograms.
The holotype, which is the specimen the species is based on, consists of several disarticulated postcranial bones.
Its feet feature downward-curved toe claws that resemble those of basal ornithomimosaurs rather than other derived Asian members of the group.
The metatarsals display the arctometatarsalian condition, a trait also found in Ornithomimus, Struthiomimus, and Gallimimus.
The shape of the pubis is more similar to North American ornithomimids than to non-ornithomimid ornithomimosaurs like Shenzhousaurus and Harpymimus.
A histological analysis of a juvenile tibia suggests the individual was a young adult still actively growing when it died.
The only known species, Q. henanensis, has a specific epithet named after the province of Henan.
Qiupalong was described in 2011 by a team of scientists from China, South Korea, Japan, and Canada led by Li Xu.
The holotype is a partial postcranial skeleton designated HGM 41HIII-0106 and is housed in the Henan Geological Museum.
In 2017, researchers led by Bradly McFeeters assigned several previously unassigned ornithomimosaur specimens to the genus Qiupalong.
The initial Qiupalong specimens referred to the genus included vertebrae, ribs, limb bones, hip bones, an ankle bone, and a pedal claw.
Specimens referred to Qiupalong sp. were not diagnostic enough for a specific species but strongly resembled bones from the holotype of Qiupalong henanensis.
Although the skull of Qiupalong is unknown, it is assumed to have been edentulous with a beak, similar to other ornithomimids.
Researchers suggest Qiupalong likely had a diet similar to Ornithomimus and Struthiomimus and may have coexisted with them with minimal competition.
Qiupalong likely coexisted with the ornithomimids Ornithomimus and possibly Struthiomimus.
Researchers hypothesize that Qiupalong may have formed multi-species assemblages similar to modern African bovids.
Qiupalong likely coexisted with three known caenagnathids: Citipes, Chirostenotes, and Caenagnathus.
Qiupalong is classified as an extinct genus of ornithomimosaurian theropod.
Phylogenetic analyses place Qiupalong in a clade with Struthiomimus and Ornithomimus, known as the "North American clade".
The "North American clade" containing Qiupalong is characterized by an acute angle between the pubic shaft and boot and an anterior extension of the pubic boot tip.
Some phylogenetic analyses, such as those by Averianov and Dieter-Sues, have recovered slightly different evolutionary positions for Qiupalong compared to other studies.
Qiupalong belongs to the family Ornithomimidae.
The type species of the genus Qiupalong is Qiupalong henanensis.
The Qiupa Formation dates to the end of the Maastrichtian stage, the final stage of the Mesozoic Era.
Despite the first described Qiupalong remains coming from Asia, the geologically oldest fossils of the genus are from Laramidia (North America).
Evidence suggests Qiupalong originated in North America and migrated to Asia near the very end of the Cretaceous Period.
The exact timing of Qiupalong's migration to Asia remains uncertain due to less thorough geochronological study of Cretaceous Asia compared to North America.
Qiupalong fossils were found in bed 34 of the Qiupa Formation, an intermediate-age layer that yielded the majority of the formation's dinosaur body fossils.
The environment where Qiupalong fossils were deposited was a braided river delta.
Qiupalong lived during the Maastrichtian stage, between 72.2 and 66 million years ago.
The earliest fossils of Qiupalong come from the Oldman Formation or the Dinosaur Park Formation.
Most confidently assigned Qiupalong remains are found in the lower half of the Dinosaur Park Formation, approximately 20 meters above the contact with the Oldman Formation.
In 2017, researchers including Philip J. Currie described postcranial ornithomimid remains from the Belly River Group in Alberta, Canada.
Specimens from Alberta were referred to the genus Qiupalong due to significant morphological similarities to the holotype.
The referral of Alberta specimens made Qiupalong the only ornithomimid genus known from both Asia and Laramidia.
Researchers did not refer the Russian Far East remains to any specific genus within Ornithomimidae.
